strengths: Extends diffusion-based intrinsic decomposition/recomposition to large-scale outdoor/autonomous-driving weather scenarios, an underexplored setting relative to prior indoor/object-level work (RGB↔X, DiffusionRenderer, IID).

Introduces two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic, 38k images; WeatherReal, 18k images) with intrinsic map annotations across diverse weather, time-of-day, and environment types, which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) mechanism is a sensible, well-motivated design (different maps need different spatial attention), supported by an ablation showing clear PSNR/LPIPS/MAE improvements and qualitative gains (e.g., correctly identifying metallic handrails).
CLIP-space interpolation for fine-grained/continuous weather control (Fig. 7) is a nice practical contribution that produces more gradual, realistic transitions than the compared baseline.

Demonstrates concrete downstream utility: measurable gains in object detection (AP75 +11.45) and semantic segmentation (mIOU +5.92) on ACDC after weather editing, which strengthens the practical motivation.
Reasonably broad set of comparisons (pixel-space editors, weather restoration methods, rendering-based methods) and inclusion of a user study (81.67% preference) to support qualitative claims.
weaknesses: The main inverse-rendering quantitative comparison (Table 3) is conducted on the authors' own WeatherSynthetic test set, which is drawn from the same distribution used to train their model; the >10dB PSNR gap over baselines (even after finetuning IID/RGB↔X on the same data) may partly reflect an inherent distributional/architectural advantage of evaluating in-domain rather than a fully fair capability comparison. Cross-domain generalization is only shown qualitatively (Fig. 9), without quantitative metrics on real, out-of-distribution data.

WeatherReal construction relies on pseudo-labels from the paper's own inverse renderer and on Flux-Kontext for weather-type alteration, raising concerns about circularity: models finetuned on WeatherReal and then evaluated qualitatively may be partly reproducing patterns from the very models used to build the dataset.

PickScore differences reported in Table 1 between the proposed method and several baselines (e.g., 20.59 vs 20.72, 20.77) are numerically very small, yet are used to support claims of superiority; no statistical significance analysis or variance is reported for this or the user study (61 participants, 8 cases).

Key architectural/training details (feature distillation implementation, progressive training heuristics for IMAA, hyperparameters for CLIP interpolation, training schedules) are deferred to supplementary material, limiting the reproducibility assessment achievable from the main text alone.

Ablation coverage is narrow: only IMAA and WeatherReal are ablated in the main paper; there is no ablation isolating the contribution of CLIP-space interpolation, the distillation loss, or the relative importance of synthetic vs. real data scale/diversity.

The acknowledged lack of temporal consistency (Fig. 12) is a real limitation for the stated autonomous-driving application, since driving perception operates on video streams; the paper only shows one qualitative failure case without deeper analysis of severity or potential mitigations.

Some baseline comparisons may be architecturally mismatched for the task (e.g., DiffusionRenderer is a video-based model applied in a single-image manner, and it's unclear whether it was properly adapted/finetuned for the outdoor driving domain vs. just applied off-the-shelf), which could understate baseline performance.

strengths: The core idea of performing weather editing in a disentangled intrinsic (material/geometry/illumination) space rather than pixel space is reasonable and addresses a real limitation of prior pixel-space weather editing methods (geometry/material drift, implausible illumination).

The paper proposes a concrete attention mechanism (IMAA) with a gating-based mask applied to text-image and image-image attention, and provides an ablation (Table 3, Fig. 11a) showing a consistent, if modest, quantitative improvement.

Two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic, 38k; WeatherReal, 18k) with intrinsic-map annotations for outdoor/driving weather scenes are introduced, filling a gap relative to existing indoor-focused intrinsic datasets (OpenRooms, Hypersim, InteriorVerse) and license-restricted MatrixCity.

Reasonably broad empirical comparison against pixel-space editors (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Instruct-Pix2Pix, WeatherWeaver), weather restoration methods (AWRaCLe, Histoformer), and inverse/forward rendering baselines (RGB↔X, IID, GeoWizard, IDArb, DiffusionRenderer), plus downstream detection/segmentation evaluation on ACDC and a small user study.
CLIP-space alpha interpolation for continuous weather intensity control is a simple and intuitive mechanism, and qualitative results (Fig. 7) suggest smoother transitions than a compared baseline.
weaknesses: Quantitative superiority in inverse/forward rendering (Table 3, >10dB PSNR gains) is measured almost entirely on the authors' own WeatherSynthetic test set, which the model was trained on and competitors were only coarsely finetuned on; this setup inherently favors the proposed method and does not demonstrate generalization advantage convincingly beyond the few qualitative real-world examples (Fig. 9).

WeatherReal, used to finetune the forward renderer for realism, is itself constructed using the paper's own inverse renderer for pseudo intrinsic maps and Flux-Kontext for weather alteration; this creates a circularity where the model is partly evaluated on a lineage of its own outputs, making claims of superiority over Flux-Kontext and other pixel-space editors less independent.

No quantitative metric is provided to validate the claimed benefit of CLIP-space alpha interpolation for fine-grained weather control (Fig. 7 is qualitative only, with no perceptual or physical measurement of intensity monotonicity or realism across alpha steps).

The user study is very small in scale (61 participants, only 8 cases) and details of the comparison protocol (which baselines, how cases were selected) are deferred to supplementary material, limiting the paper's ability to support the strong preference claim (81.67%) within the self-contained manuscript.

Key technical details are pushed to supplementary material, including the feature-distillation mechanism central to preserving SD priors (Sec 3.1), and the heuristic-guided progressive training strategy for IMAA (Sec 3.2), making the main paper's description of the method incomplete and harder to assess for correctness and reproducibility.

Equation 4 defining the attention bias M_{i,j} only depends on i (via m_i) regardless of j, which is inconsistent with it being described as a joint bias over token pairs (i,j); the formalism as written does not clearly explain how image-image vs text-image interactions are differentially biased, raising a clarity/correctness concern.

The datasets, which are a major contribution, rely on purchased 3D assets cleared for 'generative model use' and FLUX-Kontext-edited real images; licensing, exact asset provenance, and quality-control procedures for WeatherReal pseudo-labels are only briefly described, leaving reproducibility and legal/release details uncertain at review time.

Limitations are narrowly scoped to temporal consistency; other salient limitations such as dependence on accurate inverse rendering (errors propagate to forward rendering), fixed small set of weather categories in training data, and domain gap between synthetic UE5 renders and real sensor data are not discussed.

Downstream task gains (DETR/Segformer on ACDC) are reported only for a single weather-to-sunny normalization direction and a single pair of models, without baselines for how much pixel-space competitors (e.g., WeatherWeaver, Qwen-Image-Edit) improve these same downstream metrics, which would be a stronger test of the claimed real-world usefulness.

strengths: Well-motivated core idea: performing weather editing in disentangled intrinsic space (materials, geometry, illumination) rather than pixel space, which plausibly explains the improved preservation of scene structure and materials shown in qualitative comparisons.

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) mechanism is a sensible architectural contribution tailored to the specific challenge of outdoor/driving scenes (large scale variation, small distant objects), and its benefit is supported by both quantitative ablation (Table 3) and qualitative visualization (Fig. 3, 4, 11).

Introduces two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic, 38k; WeatherReal, 18k) with intrinsic map annotations targeted at autonomous driving scenarios, addressing a genuine gap since existing datasets (OpenRooms, Hypersim, MatrixCity) are indoor-focused or lack weather diversity/licensing clearance.

Broad experimental scope: comparisons against pixel-space editing (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Instruct-Pix2Pix, WeatherWeaver), weather restoration methods (AWRaCLe, Histoformer), and rendering-based methods (RGB↔X, IID, GeoWizard, IDArb, DiffusionRenderer), covering both inverse and forward rendering evaluation.
Downstream task validation on ACDC (detection with DETR, segmentation with Segformer) demonstrates practical utility beyond visual quality metrics, showing sizable absolute gains (e.g., AP75 +11.45).

Fine-grained control via CLIP-space interpolation between weather prompts is a useful practical feature not offered by comparison methods, with qualitative evidence of more natural transitions than WeatherWeaver (Fig. 7).
The paper is transparent about limitations (no temporal consistency for video), rather than overclaiming scope.
weaknesses: Quantitative inverse-rendering comparison (Table 3, the main evidence for the '10dB PSNR improvement' claim) is conducted solely on the paper's own WeatherSynthetic test set; real-world inverse rendering evaluation is only qualitative (Fig. 9), leaving the magnitude of real-world improvement unverified.

On PickScore and DINO-S metrics the proposed method is not uniformly best (Qwen-Image-Edit has higher PickScore in most weather conditions, Flux-Kontext has notably higher DINO-S), and the paper's justification for discounting these metrics, while plausible, is somewhat post-hoc rather than independently validated.

WeatherReal construction is partly circular: pseudo-labels for training/finetuning are generated using the authors' own inverse renderer plus a pretrained editing model (Flux-Kontext) for weather alteration, with quality control limited to a multimodal-model filter and unspecified manual checks; potential label bias/error propagation into training is not quantitatively assessed.

Key implementation details (feature distillation for the forward renderer, the heuristic-guided progressive training strategy for IMAA) are deferred entirely to supplementary material, making core method components not fully self-contained/verifiable in the main text.
The user study is small in scale (61 participants, 8 cases), limiting the statistical robustness of the 81.67% preference claim.
DiffusionRenderer results in Table 1 have multiple missing entries (dashes), making the rendering-based comparison incomplete for that baseline.

Ablation studies cover only IMAA and WeatherReal; other design choices (CLIP interpolation parameter α, gating mechanism variants, distillation weighting) are not ablated in the main paper, limiting insight into which components matter most.
No discussion of computational cost, inference time, or model size relative to baselines, which matters for practical adoption in downstream autonomous-driving pipelines.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: performing weather editing in intrinsic (albedo/normal/roughness/metallicity/irradiance) space rather than pixel space is a sensible way to disentangle material/geometry from weather-induced appearance changes, addressing a real limitation of prior pixel-space weather editing methods (WeatherWeaver, Instruct-Pix2Pix, etc.).

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) mechanism is a reasonable, lightweight architectural contribution to guide DiT attention using map-specific spatial cues, and the ablations (Table 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 11) show it provides measurable and interpretable gains, especially for challenging attributes like metallicity and roughness.

Extensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against a wide range of pixel-space editing baselines (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Instruct-Pix2pix, WeatherWeaver, TurboEdit), weather restoration baselines (AWRaCLe, Histoformer), and inverse-rendering/decomposition baselines (IID, RGB<->X, GeoWizard, IDArb, DiffusionRenderer) on both indoor and outdoor/driving datasets, plus downstream detection/segmentation gains on ACDC (DETR/Segformer), a user study, and substantial supplementary qualitative material.

Two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic with Unreal Engine rendering across many weather/time-of-day/environment combinations, and WeatherReal with pseudo-labeled intrinsic maps from Waymo/Kitti) fill a genuine gap, as existing intrinsic-decomposition datasets are indoor-only or lack weather diversity; the datasets are promised for release, aiding reproducibility.

The forward renderer's CLIP-space interpolation for continuous/fine-grained weather transitions (Fig. 7, Fig. 2 of supplement) is a nice practical idea, and the feature-distillation regularization to preserve the base SD3.5 prior is reasonable and ablated.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline is a fairly incremental combination of known ingredients (SD3.5 backbone, DiT, CLIP interpolation, IID/RGB<->X-style intrinsic decomposition, attention biasing akin to prior attention-guided editing) applied to a new domain (outdoor/driving weather); the core novelty largely rests on domain adaptation (new data + a masking mechanism) rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea, which somewhat limits the technical originality despite good execution.

Ground truth for outdoor/real intrinsic maps is unavailable, so WeatherReal supervision is itself generated via the model's own inverse renderer plus manual filtering with a VLM caption pipeline; this creates a degree of circularity/self-training risk (pseudo-label quality is asserted but not independently verified against any real ground truth), and quantitative real-world decomposition accuracy is therefore never rigorously demonstrated (only PSNR self-consistency across the model's own weather-invariant outputs across weather conditions, Fig. 20, which is not a ground-truth check).

Physical plausibility of the irradiance/illumination reconstruction under weather change (e.g., snow accumulation altering geometry/albedo but modeled as material-invariant, wet-road specular reflections, fog scattering physics) is not rigorously justified; the framework treats snow/rain accumulation partially as 'weather-variant' overlays but the decomposition into fixed material vs. variant illumination is a simplification for phenomena that are physically more like added occluding/reflective geometry (e.g., snow cover changes surface material properties, not just irradiance), and the paper does not discuss or quantify this approximation's error.

The downstream detection/segmentation improvement (Table 2 in main text) is evaluated only on the ACDC validation set with two models (DETR, Segformer) without further fine-tuning, and improvement magnitudes (e.g., APs from 56.56 to 61.32) are reported without confidence intervals, statistical significance testing, or discussion of possible confounds (e.g., whether the re-rendered 'sunny' images simply make the task easier in a way unrelated to genuine robustness gains, or whether hallucinated details from the diffusion model could introduce false positives).

Some evaluation metrics used for comparison (e.g., PickScore, CLIP-S, DINO-S in Table 1) are proxy metrics that do not directly quantify weather-editing correctness/geometry preservation, and no direct multi-weather intrinsic-map ground-truth benchmark for outdoor scenes is used for quantitative decomposition accuracy (Table 3 relies on synthetic WeatherSynthetic test data, which is generated by the same rendering pipeline used for training, raising possible train/test distributional similarity concerns).

The user study is small-scale (61 participants, only 8 cases), which limits statistical robustness of the reported large preference gaps (e.g., 81.67% preference), and the paper does not report variance or inter-rater agreement.

The method is explicitly limited to single-image editing and does not extend to video (acknowledged as a limitation), and failure cases under extreme occlusion (e.g., dense fog completely occluding background, Fig. 25) show that inverse rendering can hallucinate objects/geometry not actually present, which could be problematic for safety-critical downstream tasks like autonomous driving perception evaluation that the paper motivates the work with.

The paper's writing sometimes conflates 'weather editing' and 'inverse rendering' contributions; the main paper's exposition of the loss functions, training details, and dataset construction largely defers to the supplementary material, making the main text somewhat harder to assess for correctness and reproducibility without consulting many additional pages of supplementary material.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful gap: existing intrinsic-decomposition/rendering diffusion methods (IID, RGB↔X, DiffusionRenderer) target indoor or object-level scenes and do not handle large-scale outdoor driving scenes with diverse weather; the paper extends this line of work to autonomous-driving imagery.

The intrinsic map-aware attention (IMAA) is a reasonable, well-motivated architectural addition for handling the large scale variation and small/distant objects typical of driving scenes, and is supported by a qualitative visualization (Fig. 3/4) and an ablation (Tab. 3/2 in supp.) showing it improves decomposition PSNR, especially for roughness/metallicity.

The paper contributes two new datasets (WeatherSynthetic, 35K synthetic images with full intrinsic maps across many weather/time-of-day/environment combinations, and WeatherReal, 18K real images with pseudo intrinsic labels), which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.

Experimental breadth is substantial: comparisons against pixel-space editing methods (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Instruct-Pix2pix, TurboEdit, WeatherWeaver), weather-restoration methods (AWRaCLe, Histoformer), and rendering-based methods (RGB↔X, DiffusionRenderer, IID, GeoWizard, IDArb), plus a downstream-task validation on ACDC detection/segmentation and a user study, with extensive supplementary qualitative material across Waymo, KITTI, ACDC, TransWeather, DAWN, FogCityScapes, and indoor datasets.
The paper includes a frank limitations section (no temporal consistency for video) and a failure-case analysis (hallucination under heavy occlusion by fog), which is good practice.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation of the inverse renderer with ground truth (Table 3, Table 4) is only possible on synthetic data (WeatherSynthetic/InteriorVerse/Hypersim); on real-world outdoor data (WeatherReal, TransWeather, Waymo, ACDC) only qualitative comparisons are shown (Fig. 9, 21, 22), so the central claim of accurate, physically grounded decomposition is not quantitatively verified where it matters most (real driving scenes).

WeatherReal’s intrinsic-map labels are themselves generated by the paper’s own inverse renderer (and weather variants are produced via a third-party pixel-space editor, Flux-Kontext), and this same inverse renderer’s outputs are later used to argue superiority over baselines on real images (Fig. 9, 21). This creates a degree of circularity: the model is partly evaluated against pseudo-labels it helped create.

Downstream-task validation (Table 2) uses a single benchmark (ACDC) with one detector (DETR) and one segmenter (Segformer), without comparison to simpler weather-normalization baselines (e.g., just applying Flux-Kontext or a restoration method before detection) to isolate how much of the gain is attributable specifically to the intrinsic-space approach versus any successful weather normalization.

The user study is small (61 participants, 8 curated cases) and the case-selection procedure is not described in detail, leaving open the possibility of selection bias in which examples were chosen for comparison.

Table 1's cross-method comparison mixes conditioning setups (e.g., DiffusionRenderer is given an explicit environment light while the proposed method and RGB↔X are given only a text prompt), which complicates a strictly fair comparison of forward-rendering quality.

Reproducibility is hampered by substantial computational cost (multiple multi-day trainings on 8×4090/7×L40S GPUs, two separately fine-tuned SD3.5 branches, distillation, progressive IMAA pretraining) and by the synthetic dataset's dependence on purchased Unreal Engine/Fab assets, whose redistribution status is unclear; no statement about code release is given (only “datasets will be released”).

The core methodological idea (diffusion-based joint inverse/forward intrinsic rendering for editing) is a fairly direct extension of existing approaches (RGB↔X, IID, DiffusionRenderer, IntrinsicEdit) to the outdoor/weather domain; the main novel components (IMAA, CLIP-space weather interpolation, new datasets) are useful engineering contributions but represent incremental rather than conceptually new advances.

Several of the numeric improvements highlighted in the abstract/intro (e.g., "+10 dB PSNR", "87.1% relative AP75 gain") are derived from comparisons where baselines are either not fine-tuned for the target domain or evaluated only qualitatively elsewhere, which can make the reported gains appear larger than a fully matched comparison would support.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: performing weather editing in intrinsic (material/geometry/illumination) space rather than pixel space, which plausibly improves geometry and material preservation compared to pixel-space diffusion editing.

Introduces Intrinsic Map-Aware Attention (IMAA), a reasonably novel attention-biasing mechanism that uses learnable per-map embeddings and DINO features to guide DiT attention toward regions relevant to each intrinsic property; ablations (Tab. 2/3, Fig. 11a) show it measurably improves decomposition quality, especially for fine geometric detail and small/distant objects.

Contributes two new large-scale datasets (WeatherSynthetic: 35K/38K synthetic driving images with full intrinsic map annotations across many weather/time-of-day/environment combinations, and WeatherReal: 18K real-world images with inverse-rendered pseudo intrinsic maps), filling a genuine gap since existing intrinsic datasets are almost exclusively indoor or lack weather diversity.

Extensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against multiple pixel-space editors (Flux-Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Instruct-Pix2pix, WeatherWeaver, TurboEdit), weather-restoration baselines (AWRaCLe, Histoformer), and rendering-based baselines (RGB↔X, DiffusionRenderer, IID, GeoWizard, IDArb) on both indoor and outdoor/driving benchmarks, with quantitative metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/MAE, PickScore/CLIP-S/DINO-S), a user study, and downstream task validation (DETR/SegFormer performance gains on ACDC).

Reasonably thorough ablations (IMAA, WeatherReal fine-tuning, feature distillation, heuristic progressive training, CLIP-space interpolation strategy) that support the design choices rather than merely asserting them.

Demonstrates non-trivial generalization to out-of-distribution real data (Waymo, KITTI, TransWeather, ACDC, DAWN, FogCityScapes, and even non-driving photos), and the paper is transparent about a concrete failure mode (background hallucination under heavy occlusion) rather than hiding limitations.
Clear articulation of scope and honest discussion of the single-image/no-temporal-consistency limitation, with a plausible pointer to future work rather than overclaiming video capability.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline (two large fine-tuned SD3.5 backbones plus an IMAA module plus a distillation stage) is computationally heavy, and the paper does not report inference/training compute costs, memory footprint, or runtime comparisons against the pixel-space baselines it compares to, which matters for assessing practical usefulness.

WeatherReal's intrinsic-map labels are pseudo-labels generated by the paper's own inverse renderer and only spot-checked visually ("check the quality manually"); using self-generated pseudo-labels to fine-tune the same family of models risks confirmation bias/error accumulation that is not independently validated against any real ground truth.

Quantitative rendering-quality numbers, while better than baselines, are still moderate in absolute terms (e.g., Normal PSNR ~25 dB, Roughness/Metallic PSNR ~24-29 dB) and the paper does not report confidence intervals, variance across scenes, or statistical significance for these comparisons or for the small-scale user study (61 participants, 8 cases).

The comparison in Table 1 shows Flux-Kontext achieving a substantially higher DINO-S than the proposed method (85.50 vs 73.63), which the paper explains post hoc as Flux-Kontext simply failing to edit the image; this metric result somewhat undercuts the framing that DINO-S reflects structural fidelity and is not fully reconciled quantitatively.

The fine-grained interpolation control (CLIP-space alpha shifting) is only demonstrated qualitatively (Fig. 7, supplementary Fig. 2); no quantitative metric (e.g., smoothness/monotonicity of intensity, consistency across alpha steps) is provided to substantiate the controllability claims beyond visual inspection.

The core technical ingredients (diffusion-based intrinsic decomposition/recomposition, attention-based spatial guidance, CLIP direction interpolation for controllable generation) are each conceptually close to prior works (RGB↔X, DiffusionRenderer, IntrinsicEdit, WeatherWeaver, prior CLIP-direction editing methods); the novelty is more in the combination, adaptation to large-scale outdoor scenes, and the new datasets than in a fundamentally new technique, which is acceptable but should be described with calibrated novelty claims.

Dataset release logistics (e.g., licensing status of purchased Fab/Unreal Engine 5 assets used to render WeatherSynthetic, and whether raw asset geometry or only rendered outputs will be shared) are not clearly addressed, which is relevant for reproducibility and community reuse of the promised dataset release.
